Insurance is unusual in that its costs are only estimated when the price is set. Most businesses know what a product costs before they sell it. title: UNH student organizations celebrate Hispanic Heritage Month with campus-wide events - The Charger Bulletin
content: Hispanic Heritage Month is underway, and student organizations across campus are preparing cultural, artistic and community-centered events. From silent discos to animation displays, resident student organizations (RSOs) are highlighting Hispanic culture, honoring community traditions and bringing students together. The Myatt Center for Diversity and Inclusion anchors the programming each year, but this fall, student-led organizations are taking an especially active role. The Latin American Student Association (LASA), the university’s Animation Club and Greek-letter organizations are collaborating to create one of the most event-packed calendars the university has seen in recent years. A LASA official said that Hispanic Heritage Month is more than a celebration; it is about unity, identity and honoring people who shape Hispanic culture. In a statement given by LASA president Nikki Rosario, a senior marine biology student, and vice president Steven Ojeda, a junior psychology student with a focus in forensics, said: “Hispanic Heritage Month is not just about celebrating one culture but about celebrating our different identities while recognizing what brings us together. We want our members and everyone who attends our events to feel seen, understood, and proud to be part of such a beautiful culture,” they said. “El Apagon represents what LASA is about: Bringing people together through culture and community.” The students said “El Apagon” is one of their favorite events this year, inspired by Bad Bunny’s song and the blackout scene in the 2021 movie, “In the Heights.” Both references use darkness as a symbol of community resilience, something LASA members say they hope to bring to campus. The Animation Club will co-host LA Animación de Cultura with LASA on Oct. 6, focusing on Hispanic representation in animation. Animation Club president Gian Rodriguez, a senior graphic & digital design student, shared why this event matters. “As a Mexican and Puerto Rican student, it is amazing to see fellow Hispanic animators mold and shape what Hispanic culture is in animation,” he said. The event will explore both positive representation and harmful stereotypes in animated media. Students will also have the chance to create their own character inspired by Hispanic Culture. “We feel it is important to showcase and talk about the involvement of culturally rich communities in animation, as they are part of the beauty that helps make such captivating pieces of media,” Rodriguez said. Students will have opportunities to engage with art, music, film, dance and cultural education all led by organizations committed to uplifting Hispanic voices. From LASA’s community-centered programming to the Animation Club’s creative showcase, this year’s Hispanic Heritage Month events highlight the diversity, resilience and joy of Hispanic culture at the university. title: Food Among the Trees - University of New Hampshire
content: ‌New Hampshire is more than 80% forested, second ‌in coverage only to Maine in the U.S. The Adaptive ‌Agroforestry Principles and Teaching (ADAPT) program is leveraging this important resource through the testing and teaching of agroforestry concepts and methods, work that will support local farming and sustain a stronger regional food system. Agroforestry expands agricultural opportunities by embracing, rather than seeking to overcome, the tree-filled landscape. ADAPT is a collaborative effort led by Heidi Asbjornsen, professor of natural resources and the environment, that also includes researchers at Yale University, Dartmouth College, and 12 operating farms. ADAPT works with three primary types of agroforestry. Forest farming grows shade-tolerant crops under an existing tree canopy. Food forests contain food-producing plants of varying heights, such as nut trees, berry bushes, and herbs, within the same space. And silvopasture provides livestock pasturing and grazing space among trees. Unlike most fully cleared pasture and crop lands, all offer welcoming habitats for beneficial insects, pollinators, and wildlife. “Agroforestry can increase crop diversity and sustainability, providing farmers and growers with more resilience in changing conditions as well as expanding income-generating opportunities,” says Asbjornsen. “But agroforestry systems are complex to manage. Education and extension are critical parts of ADAPT so that we can share our research-based insights with the community.” Copyright © 2026 , University of New Hampshire. All rights reserved.

title: Chipotle Opens Near UNH in Durham, New Hampshire - Hoodline
content: Chipotle Mexican Grill is planting a new flag steps from the University of New Hampshire campus, with a restaurant planned at 7 Mill Road, Suite A, in Durham on Sept. 29, 2026. It follows an Aug. 19 opening in Braintree, Massachusetts, marking a fresh push by the burrito chain into the Boston-Manchester corridor. The Durham location sits near the UNH campus, according to Boston Real Estate Times. The Braintree restaurant, at 165 Pearl St., opened Aug. 19, giving Chipotle two fresh footholds in the region within about six weeks of each other. UNH provides a substantial nearby campus backdrop, though its degree-seeking enrollment in Durham dipped from 13,360 in fall 2024 to 12,819 in fall 2025. The university also said it received 2,471 first-year deposits for fall 2026, nearly 4% more than a year earlier. The figures offer a snapshot of the student population close to the new restaurant, without indicating how many students will become customers. UNH’s Durham enrollment history and fall 2026 admissions update provide the counts. The Durham address falls within Durham Landing, a retail property marketed by Eastern Retail as having 10,700 square feet of existing endcap space and redeveloped small-shop units ranging from 1,730 to 7,885 square feet, subdividable to fit different tenants. Eastern Retail's listing describes the property as ideal for full-service and quick-service restaurants, along with fitness and medical uses, suggesting Chipotle is one of several types of businesses the site was built to attract. Durham's own planning records point to a larger redevelopment underway in the same area. A site-plan page on the town's website identifies a Mill Plaza project at 5 Mill Road involving architectural improvements to the building facade and other exterior renovations, with 5-7 Mill Road LLC listed as the property owner. A separate site-plan review application on file with the town references 7 Mill Road, Unit L, as part of that broader Mill Plaza redevelopment, which the filing describes as including 108 residential units, 258 beds, and roughly 80,250 square feet of total commercial space once complete. The Mill Plaza property has a longer planning history distinct from the current restaurant opening. In 2022, Durham’s Planning Board denied a redevelopment application for Mill Plaza, and the state Housing Appeals Board affirmed that decision later that year. Town records identify 5 and 7 Mill Road as being in Durham’s Central Business zoning district. That history puts the new storefront within a site that has previously drawn formal land-use review, but does not establish that Chipotle’s tenancy was part of the earlier proposal. The town’s account of the 2022 denial and its update on the appeal document those decisions. Both the Braintree and Durham restaurants are expected to create employment opportunities in the region, and Chipotle is hiring for both, with each location carrying approximately 30 open positions, per the same report. Once open, both restaurants are set to run daily from 10:45 a.m. to 10 p.m., the outlet reports. The expansion adds to Chipotle's presence in the broader Boston and New Hampshire markets, as the chain continues building out its footprint across the region. The two local openings also come amid a wider company expansion. Chipotle ended 2025 with 4,056 restaurants and opened 334 company-owned locations that year, while comparable restaurant sales fell 1.7%. The company forecast 350 to 370 new openings in 2026. The figures place the Braintree and Durham restaurants within a national growth push, even as the chain reported a year-over-year decline in sales at established locations. Chipotle’s 2025 results and 2026 outlook give the companywide totals. Chipotle is also promoting new and limited-time menu offerings across the Boston-Manchester region, including pollo asado, a grilled chicken option seasoned with garlic and Mexican spices and finished with cilantro and citrus, alongside chili lime chips seasoned with lime and chili peppers. The chain is pairing that with a high-protein menu for the market, featuring items ranging from 15 to 81 grams of protein, such as a double high-protein bowl, a high protein-high fiber bowl, and a high-protein cup, plus a single chicken taco starting at $3.50. Chipotle Rewards members can also tap into monthly food rewards and customizable birthday benefits, while new members can receive free chips and guac with a purchase. The chain additionally offers family meal options built for groups eating at home, and local organizations can use Chipotle's fundraising program, which helps groups raise money for community causes through restaurant-based fundraising events. For the roughly 60 workers Chipotle hopes to hire across the two new restaurants, the company points to a broader benefits package. Employees are eligible for a crew bonus program that can provide the chance to earn an additional month's pay each year, along with a debt-free college degree program. title: Counting the Recovery of New Hampshire Bats - University of New Hampshire
content: New Hampshire bats have been in crisis for years. Beginning in 2009, a fatal fungal disease known as white-nose syndrome devastated all five of the state’s cave-hibernating bat species. Researchers and Extension specialists in COLSA are now teaming up with the NH Fish and Game Department and Granite State landowners to support one of the state’s key programs supporting the conservation and recovery of the remaining Laura Kloepper, associate professor of biological sciences, leads UNH’s Ecological Acoustics and Behavior Lab, studying how animals use acoustics to navigate the world and how we, in turn, can use acoustics to monitor them. Acoustic technology has gotten both better and less expensive in recent years, and it can now be applied to NH Bat Counts. “NH Bat Counts has been active for a long time, and we’re joining it now to contribute our experience with advanced technology to expand and improve data gathering,” says Kloepper. “The work is vital for tracking bat abundance and providing insights to protect them and their habitats.” Why do bats matter to us? Estimates vary, but studies indicate bats contribute at least $3.7 billion and potentially more than $50 billion in insect pest control for U.S. agriculture alone every year. Without them, controlling pests becomes more costly and losses for New Hampshire industries such as agriculture and forestry increase. White-nose syndrome was first detected in hibernating bats in New York State in 2006. When it arrived in New Hampshire in 2009, surveys of the four largest caves and mines favored by bats for hibernation counted 3,230 of these flying mammals. By 2011, that number had plummeted to 16. For reasons that remain poorly understood, some species of bats elsewhere have proven to be more resilient to the fungus that causes white-nose syndrome. And some colonies are beginning to grow once again, though their numbers remain much smaller than pre-disease. “There has been growth in some of the maternity colonies over the last few years,” says Haley Andreozzi ’13G, Extension state specialist and Extension professor of wildlife conservation. “In 2022, we had a colony with more than 700 individuals, the first time we’ve measured one that large. There’s a long way to go — pre-disease, some colonies had thousands of bats — but we’re beginning to see some small but needed wins for the bats.” The NH Fish and Game Department, NH Audubon, and U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service launched NH Bat Counts in 2012 to find and quantify the survivors. The program monitors summer bat colonies in barns, attics, steeples, and other structures where female bats gather and give birth to their young during the warmer months. NH Bat Counts is now spearheaded by Sandra Houghton ’04G, wildlife diversity biologist with the NH Fish and Game Department, and Andreozzi. Houghton and Andreozzi have worked together to extend and formalize the program over the past half dozen years. “The data from NH Bat Counts volunteers furthers our knowledge about the location, species, and status of bat colonies in New Hampshire,” says Houghton. “It helps us prioritize conservation efforts while also creating a network of bat ambassadors.” Kloepper’s work will make it possible to look at trends in the acoustic energy produced by the bats to get a sense of movement within the colonies, the timing of pup independence, how environmental conditions such as weather impact pup emergence and roost shifting, and more. The recorders will also allow volunteers to obtain nightly population estimates far more efficiently than previously possible. Andreozzi notes the interest and enthusiasm of the volunteers, who enjoy learning about how valuable their barns and other structures are for bats and contributing to the efforts to protect bat colonies. Now, Kloepper’s expertise and recorder technologies will enable the volunteers to help even more. She has also involved her students in the research and outreach efforts, and eight undergraduates have formed a “bat count” team devoted to devising better ways to count bats for conservation. “It’s a great example of how research is being done at UNH,” says Kloepper. “All parties — researchers, students, Extension, and state experts — are out in the New Hampshire community, working together toward a common goal.” Copyright © 2026 , University of New Hampshire. title: What Are UNH Stock Investors Betting On? - Trefis
content: UnitedHealth (UNH) stock trades at 22.5 times its past year’s adjusted earnings, which are normalized net income with stock-based pay added back. That multiple leaves little room for error after three years of shrinking operating margins, sitting near the stock’s 10-year median despite fundamentally weaker profitability. But the price looks different against the profit expected for fiscal 2026 and fiscal 2027. So what are UnitedHealth investors betting on? UnitedHealth investors are betting on wider margins in fiscal 2026 and fiscal 2027. A P/E is the share price divided by a year of profit. On the consensus forecast for fiscal 2026, today’s price is 19.0 times earnings. On the fiscal 2027 forecast, it is 16.8 times, beside 22.5 times for the past year. The consensus forecast has profit rising 12.9% from fiscal 2026 to fiscal 2027. Sales in the forecast rise just 3.0% over the same year. Profit only outgrows sales when a company keeps more of each dollar of sales. So the forecast P/Es are real only if UnitedHealth’s net margin widens—an expansion that ultimately depends on reversing the slide in its operating margins. Not over the last three years. Operating margin is the share of sales left after medical and running costs. At UnitedHealth, it fell each year, from 8.8% three years ago to 4.8% now. UnitedHealth’s margins did widen in the second quarter of fiscal 2026. Operating earnings grew 55% from a year earlier on flat revenue. Management credited product and portfolio changes, and said better results in Medicare Advantage put its UnitedHealthcare business ahead of expectations. Medical costs that quarter were also flattered by $860 million in favorable reserve adjustments—mostly developed from earlier in 2026—giving a substantial one-time boost to that 55% operating jump. Management then raised its fiscal 2026 guidance for adjusted earnings per share to $19.50 to $20. The consensus forecast of $19.95 per share for fiscal 2026 is near the top of that guidance. Management called that range the right baseline to build toward its long-term earnings growth goal of 13% to 16%. The forecast’s fiscal 2027 profit growth is at about the low end of that goal. So the forecast sits close to management’s own targets, at the upper end for fiscal 2026. Mostly in medical costs, starting with UnitedHealth’s commercial benefits business. Management said commercial costs are stubbornly high and rising above expectations. Management also moved the full recovery of commercial margins past 2027. If those costs do not ease, the consensus forecast for fiscal 2027 profit is more likely to fall than rise. Medicare Advantage is the other major risk, despite driving the second quarter’s beat. Management said its own changes to benefits, care management and networks were a primary reason Medicare costs grew less than expected. Management added that the slower growth is not a turning point, and that Medicare costs are continuing at high levels. If Medicare cost growth speeds up again, fiscal 2027 profit could fall short of the consensus forecast. The medical care ratio is the share of premiums UnitedHealth spends on care. Management expects it at 88.1% for fiscal 2026, plus or minus a quarter of a percentage point. UnitedHealth reports its third quarter on October 13, 2026. Management said it would probably update its Medicare cost estimate then. If UnitedHealth’s margins recover as the forecast assumes, the P/Es on the consensus forecast are a fair picture of today’s price. Commercial medical costs are the likeliest place for that recovery to fall short. Management has already pushed back the commercial margin recovery. If those costs stay high, the stock is riskier than it looks. At current levels, you are paying for margin recovery before it has fully materialized. An upward revision to the 2026 medical care ratio in the October report would indicate that this recovery is taking longer than projected. Before you decide on UNH, consider a better choice. title: Marlborough’s Ava VanBuskirk finds her footing playing soccer at University of New Hampshire - Community Advocate
content: Ava VanBuskirk (Ryan Moran/University of New Hampshire) DURHAM, NH – AUGUST 12: UNH Women’s Soccer hosts the 2026 Media Day at the UNH Field House on August 12, 2026 in Durham, New Hampshire. (Photo by Alex Miller) Ava VanBuskirk during her time in Marlborough (Photo/Jesse Kucewicz) Ava VanBuskirk during her time in Marlborough (Photo/Jesse Kucewicz) MARLBOROUGH — In dramatic fashion, Frank Vana captured his t… MARLBOROUGH – Every year, Meredith Harris parks at Kelleher … Ava VanBuskirk (Ryan Moran/University of New Hampshire) MARLBOROUGH – When Ava VanBuskirk left Marlborough High School with 100-plus career goals, she hoped her success in finding the back of the net would continue at her next stop: the University of New Hampshire. Her freshman year, she played 41 minutes. She played 65 minutes in her sophomore year, but injuries to both knees cut her season short and required separate surgeries. She spent five months rehabbing only to play 10 minutes of the Wildcats’ final spring game. But those 10 minutes were plenty to show her enormous potential. “She made a huge impact on the team in those 10 minutes,” head coach Steve Welham told the Community Advocate. “It was awesome to see. Ava has carried that impact into this season.” In the team’s first four games this fall, VanBuskirk averaged 37 minutes but didn’t figure in any of the team’s goals. Then, over three days, she scored her first two collegiate goals in a 4-1 win over Northeastern, followed by another goal in a 4-2 win over Merrimack. DURHAM, NH – AUGUST 12: UNH Women’s Soccer hosts the 2026 Media Day at the UNH Field House on August 12, 2026 in Durham, New Hampshire. (Photo by Alex Miller) “Ava has been a very positive story for us,” said Welham. “She has developed each year and is taking this opportunity and really running with it. She can fly – she has a great engine, great endurance, and she’s just really coming into her own.” The rehabilitation process was hardly sunshine and rainbows for VanBuskirk. “It was hard mentally. I had never been a player who was on the sidelines to watch. That was a big transition going from always playing and soccer always being my outlet, and then not having that,” said VanBuskirk, an aspiring elementary school teacher. “My teammates were awesome and always included me. It was about finding my role on the team in a different way. … I took the role of being on the bench and cheering as loud as I could.” VanBuskirk went to physical therapy three times a week and worked with different trainers to regain her strength and mobility. Those grueling workouts are now paying off. She’s been electric on the field, said Welham. “She’s two-footed. She loves to go 1-versus-1 on a defender,” he said. “She’s technical, she’s dynamic, and her game is built around pace and dynamic movement on and off the ball. Her energy and positivity coming off the bench have just elevated the team to another level.” Ava VanBuskirk during her time in Marlborough (Photo/Jesse Kucewicz) Her first collegiate goal – a rebound off an initial shot taken by Elizabeth Finn – was “such a surreal feeling,” she said. At the time of the score, VanBuskirk was focused on getting back on the field; scoring was simply an added bonus. “I was really focusing on coming back from my injury and trying to get back to where I was before, so when I got my opportunity to get on the field and play, I took it and did my best,” VanBuskirk said. “Instead of stressing myself out, I focused on having fun and why I play the sport. It really helped that the girls around me supported me and were excited for me, along with my family, friends, and coaches.” Thirteen minutes after her first collegiate goal, VanBuskirk scored another. Each time, her “large soccer family” – including her mother Pam, a Marlborough soccer alum; her brother Joey; and her aunt, uncle, and cousin, who all played collegiately – were there to celebrate in the stands. Ava VanBuskirk during her time in Marlborough (Photo/Jesse Kucewicz) “Soccer has always been a part of my life,” VanBuskirk said. “I looked up to my brother and older cousins, and we played soccer on every family outing and summer trip, always with a soccer ball. It was nice being able to grow up with everyone, especially my brother, because he’s always been my biggest role model, and I always wanted to make him proud.” Unlock the power of local outreach with our platform! title: Giant pumpkins grow from Durham retirement community project with UNH - Foster's Daily Democrat
content: DURHAM — Giant pumpkins were grown by residents of Brookdale Spruce Wood, a retirement community, and one will be entered in the Deerfield Fair. The community project brought together people from Brookdale Spruce Wood, the University of New Hampshire, families, friends and neighbors, resulting in five very big pumpkins. The Brookdale Spruce Wood UNH giant pumpkin project began in 2025, when a photograph of an enormous pumpkin caught residents' attention during a presentation about “Our Backyard” by resident Jim Cross, 79, an outdoor enthusiast and nature lover. Inspired by the image, Cross and fellow resident, friend and outdoor partner-in-crime Daniel Reich, 86, began researching how to grow a giant pumpkin of their own. Their efforts led them to Christopher Hernandez, assistant professor of plant breeding at the University of New Hampshire. With his guidance, Cross and Reich laid out and rototilled three pumpkin patches. They then made 10 trips to Coyote Spring Farm in Lee to haul horse manure back to the patches. With Hernandez's help, they obtained seeds from two prize-winning pumpkins, including one grown in 2018 by Steve Geddes of Boscawen that weighed 2,528 pounds (a U.S. record for six years). On June 5, Cross, Reich and Hernandez planted four pumpkin seedlings – initially grown by UNH students – in each of the three pumpkin patches surrounding Brookdale Spruce Wood. Geddes donated retired paper-mill conveyor-belt squares to serve as sturdy “beds” for the pumpkins. He and Hernandez also taught the team about support and cushioning, including the use of sand and pool noodles. Old sheets provided shade and protection from the sun. Cross and Reich tended the plants every day and with Hernandez's guidance, the team narrowed the field to the two strongest plants in each patch and carefully assisted with pollination. Over the next 16 weeks, throughout July, August and September, the once-tiny seeds/seedlings grew rapidly. The project soon attracted attention beyond Brookdale Spruce Wood. Members of the New Hampshire Giant Pumpkin Association paid the community a visit. Neighbors from the surrounding community stopped by during their daily walks to check on the pumpkins, while visiting family and friends did the same. Those regular visits sparked conversations and new friendships. The largest pumpkin, affectionately named “Frankenstein,” reached an impressive 1,000 pounds before splitting open! Despite the major disappointment, the project continued. Brookdale Spruce Wood residents helped name the four remaining pumpkins: The group plans to officially weigh the pumpkins on Wednesday, Sept. 30. The winning pumpkin will be sent to the Deerfield Fair to compete on Thursday, Oct. 1 against approximately 30 other pumpkins in the heaviest giant-pumpkin and/or prettiest giant-pumpkin competition.

title: Mel Rines ’47 Makes $1M Gift to Bolster Key Priority in UNH Strategic Plan - University of New Hampshire
content: Mel Rines ’47 (seated) recently made a $1M gift to UNH. Mel Rines ’47 recently made his largest one-time gift ever to UNH, a $1 million contribution that will impact students from a wide swath of disciplines and academic areas while advancing a key pillar of President Elizabeth Chilton’s strategic plan for the university. Rines – who is among the university’s most generous benefactors – recently made the gift to bolster Chilton’s focus on interdisciplinary education and research excellence, support that will both help advance one of four strategic priorities in Chilton’s “One UNH: Roadmap to 2030” initiative and is also a seamless match for Rines’ personal philosophy. “Be bold, aim high, and have fun” is a favorite motto of Rines, who graduated from UNH as a psychology major and U.S. Naval fighter pilot before ultimately spending his career in the investment business. He had lofty goals from the start, with a desire for independence and helping mankind, and was guided by a personal mantra – “success on my terms.” So, it’s only fitting that his latest gift lands at the intersection of flexibility and innovation at UNH. It is the largest contribution to UNH for Rines, who has donated steadily since his initial support in 1982, extending a deep relationship with the university that began during his days as a student. Rines’ tenure at UNH was interrupted when he joined the Navy and trained as a fighter pilot during World War II. After graduating from UNH, he went on to study optometry and joined a Naval reserve fighter squadron. That squadron was the first to be recalled at the start of the Korean War in 1950 where he flew the first jets in active combat off the aircraft carrier USS Boxer. His years traveling and meeting others as a U.S. Navy fighter pilot broadened his thinking about career opportunities. Leaving the Navy, Rines passed on an opportunity to pilot commercial airplanes, embarking instead on a new challenge, a career in the investment world. Rines, now 102, went on to carve out a successful and fulfilling 46-year career beginning as a retail broker, culminating in international investment banking with the firm that first employed him, Kidder Peabody. He worked closely with the development banks and the International Monetary Fund to help developing nations access international credit markets to help fuel their infrastructure projects and economic development. Rines first reconnected with UNH in 1982 by seeding and co-directing the International Private Enterprise Center at the Whittemore School of Business and Economics, now Paul College. “UNH has always been dear to me,” Rines says. “I’ve always been so fond of the professors and the students.” Rines’ previous giving also focused on university-wide opportunities. His gifts led to the creation of offerings like the Rines Student Angel Investment Fund and the International Changemakers Grant (formally Student International Service Initiative) – programs that encourage involvement from students from all majors. “My father wanted to create innovative programs that would go across departments of the university,” his daughter, Marcy Venezia, says. “You see that with the Rines Angel Fund where you don’t have to be a business major to become a part of it.” Indeed, the Rines Angel Fund – a hands-on program that immerses students in the realm of early-stage investing – is housed within the Peter T. Paul College of Business and Economics, but participation is encouraged across all majors. Similarly, the International Changemaker Grant, which allows students to travel globally and work on sustainability projects that establish relationships with international communities of need, is open to UNH students from any college. The Rines Angel Fund gives students real-world experience within the angel fund ecosystem and the International Changemaker Grant gives them a chance to contribute to significant sustainability work while traveling to areas of the world they may not otherwise get to see. David Rines, Mel’s son, says one of the goals of the changemaker grant was “for students who might not have left New Hampshire before to have an opportunity to do something really meaningful outside the US.” “I think both the Rines Angel Fund and the International Changemaker Grant are about giving students real-world experience outside the classroom that make a real difference in terms of their career opportunities. It’s so gratifying to feel like these students have opportunities that I didn’t see growing up,” says David Rines. Adds Venezia, “It was that emphasis on moving away from just straight academics into real-world experience that always resonated with my father.” Rines’ focus through it all has been to create as many opportunities as possible for UNH students. He and his family have been able to witness up-close how much of an impact the Rines Angel Fund and International Changemaker Grant have had in terms of opening real-world career opportunities to students. So, it’s no wonder Rines became immediately intrigued after hearing about President Chilton’s Roadmap to 2030 priorities. In November of 2025, The Rines family hosted Chilton and learned more about her vision, a meeting that ultimately inspired the $1 million commitment to advance the interdisciplinary education and research effort. “It was gratifying to hear about all the work that was already underway on the Roadmap and this gift felt like something that would further support President Chilton and her initiatives while also being in line with my father’s interest in innovation and interdisciplinary learning,” says David Rines. “We’re excited to see where this can go.” Rines’ UNH affection runs deep. He has been a dedicated volunteer at UNH for more than two decades, is a former chair of the UNH Foundation Board, and currently serves on the emeriti board, the Rines Student Angel Investment Fund investment committee, and the International Changemakers Grant committee. Beyond The Rines Angel Fund and the International Changemaker Grant, Rines’ generosity has led to the establishment of several additional funds, including the S. Melvin and Mary Jo Rines Art Exhibit Fund and the Mel Rines ’47 Fellowship Fund. Mel and his wife, Mary Jo Rines, were honored in 2007 with UNH’s Hubbard Family Award for Service to Philanthropy, the highest honor bestowed upon those whose philanthropic leadership has strengthened the state, its communities, and the university. Through all of that, David Rines and his sister have long witnessed their father’s commitment to both people-centered philanthropy and his alma mater. His legacy at UNH was cemented long before this most recent gift, but the contribution to interdisciplinary education and research excellence is yet another illustration of that combination that will carry forward for years to come. Venezia says, “My father is not one to say, ‘I did that.’ He’s not a showman in that way. He always quietly encourages the people around him, and he’s done that with us, and he’s doing that now with his ideas about philanthropy.” Copyright © 2026 , University of New Hampshire. title: New poll shows Gov. Phil Scott leading Amanda Janoo by 10 points - VTDigger
content:
Prepare for Vermont’s Nov. 3 general election with VTDigger’s 2026 Election Guide. Get the latest reporting from towns across Vermont delivered each morning in Daily Digger, our free newsletter. Gov. Phil Scott holds a 10-point lead over progressive Democrat Amanda Janoo in a poll released Monday, a striking reversal from a separate survey last week that showed the race in a statistical tie. Vermont Public’s 2026 Poll reported Scott is leading Janoo by 10 points, 42% to 32%. These results reflect a 16-point swing from Friday’s Green Mountain State Poll by the University of New Hampshire, which, based on margin of error in the survey, declared a “statistical tie,” with Janoo leading the race 49% to 43%. “Public polling has always undervalued the Governor’s support,” Scott’s campaign spokesperson Emma Shouldice wrote in a statement Monday. She added that the Vermont Public poll was “much better” than the UNH survey, but still discounted Scott. Among likely voters — the Vermonters polled who said they would “definitely” or “probably vote” — the margin remained 10 points with the incumbent Scott leading 44% to 34%. Sixteen percent of those likely voters remain unsure or have no opinion, according to the poll. Vermont Public’s poll also reported former Democratic Lt. Gov. Molly Gray leading Republican incumbent John Rodgers by eight points in the lieutenant governor race. U.S. Rep. Becca Balint, D-Vt. is leading the congressional race against Republican nominee Gerald Malloy, 43% to 28%. Longtime Vermont political journalist Chris Graff called last week’s UNH poll an “outlier.” “I think the Vermont Public poll is a little more in line with how those of us who follow this closely see the race, which is that Governor Scott maintains a lead,” he said in an interview Monday. “Amanda Janoo has a strong following but is largely unknown.” Scott remained the most popular governor in the country as of a July report by the firm Morning Consult. Vermont Public’s polling reported that Scott held a 45% approval rating, a 15-point decline since their last poll in 2022. UNH also reported a 47% approval rating, which had decreased by five points since July. Graff said that declining approval ratings are to be expected for Scott, but that the drop could be explained by Scott not having “solved the problems that are facing the state of Vermont.” Alternatively, he said, Scott’s ratings could be explained by national sentiment. “The national mood is such that if you have an ‘R’ beside your name — even if you’re someone like Phil Scott — that ‘R’ is an anchor,” Graff said. Twenty percent is a significant number of uncertain voters this close to the election, Graff said. He expects that debates will “make a difference,” but that Janoo doesn’t have the “money or organization” to reach the “larger number of voters” across the state who are undecided. “We haven’t seen (the candidates debate) yet,” Graff said. “She is not yet defined in the public. title: Can Surplus-Food Apps Have Too Much Competition? - University of New Hampshire
content: Apps that let businesses sell surplus food at a discount in “surplus bags” have become a popular way to keep edible food out of landfills while giving consumers access to lower-cost meals and groceries. But new research from Wei Wei, assistant professor of decision sciences at UNH's Peter T. Paul College of Business and Economics, suggests the results aren't always so straightforward. While surplus-food platforms can benefit businesses, consumers, and the environment, the researchers found that when competition becomes too intense, food waste can rise and retailer profits can fall. One reason: getting surplus food out of a store doesn't necessarily mean it all gets eaten. If consumers receive more food than they need, the extra can still end up wasted at home. In a study published in Decision Sciences, Wei and co-author Zhangchen Hu, assistant professor at California State University, Fullerton, built a mathematical model of how retailers balance traditional in-store sales with sales of discounted surplus bags through apps such as Too Good To Go. Their analysis suggests that while the platforms can create significant benefits, those benefits depend heavily on local market conditions. "The app itself is helping, but what we're really investigating is whether it's always helping in the way it's intended," Wei says. "The result is not automatic. Under certain scenarios, competition can benefit consumers, retailers, and society, but under others, more competition may not be a good thing." Too Good To Go launched in the U.S. in late 2020 and is now used nationwide. As Wei and Hu explored the platform's challenges, they spoke with participating retailers. "I went down to Boston and interviewed a few retailers that participate in the app. They told me it helped them clear out edible food that otherwise might have been thrown away or composted," Wei says. "But a grocery store manager in Cambridge told me participating can also be challenging.  With perishable foods such as prepared foods, baked goods and produce, they don't know how much they'll have left at the end of the day. They have to decide how many surplus bags to make available on the app before they know what their in-store demand will be." Make too many surplus bags available, and retailers risk missing higher-margin in-store purchases. Make too few available, and they may miss the chance to recover value from food that would otherwise go unsold. Pricing adds another wrinkle. Under the platform’s rules, a bag's price is tied to the value of the food inside, so a higher-priced bag is required to contain food with a higher total value. In many cases, that also means more food in the bag. For example, if a bag's price can be no more than 40% of the food's value, a $4 bag would contain at least $10 worth of food. That may suit consumers who need more food but leave others with more than they can use. Competition further complicates those decisions. With more businesses offering surplus bags to the same pool of customers, retailers must decide how to price their bags and how much food to set aside while also accounting for what other participating businesses are doing. "I would expect competition to always help," Wei says. "At first, as competition increases, food waste goes down. But there's a point where that changes. When competition becomes too intense, food waste starts to increase." Consumers continue to benefit as competition increases, but retailers don't share in those gains. The model found that retailer profits decline as more businesses compete on the platform. Wei says the findings aren't an argument against surplus-food platforms. Researchers found many situations where competition among retailers produces a "win-win-win"— higher consumer benefits, higher retailer profits, and lower food waste. In the model, this can occur when surplus bags are offered at a substantial discount and consumers strongly value the bags. The key is understanding the market. A bakery that's one of a dozen on the app in its neighborhood faces very different conditions than one with few nearby competitors, and the model suggests the right pricing and bag-size decisions can differ sharply between the two. "Retailers should not view these platforms as an automatic solution for their surplus food," Wei says. "They need to think strategically about pricing and bag size, while considering their projected in-store demand, how much food their customers actually need and how many other retailers are competing nearby." The platforms themselves can play a role, too. The model suggests that adjusting discount levels based on market conditions could help reduce food waste and, in some cases, improve retailer profits. Helping consumers better understand the value of surplus bags could also improve outcomes. Wei says future research could examine the platform's decisions more directly and how it can balance the interests of businesses, consumers, and food waste reduction. "Overall, their intention is good, and what they are doing is good," Wei says. "The question is how much good they can do and whether they can achieve the best outcome."
